case_title: Kunjumon @ Unni v. State of Kerala
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated for the deceased (Annamma); the defence contended the accused was a total stranger to PW-2 Lidiya
statutory_provisions: IPC s.449; IPC s.397; IPC s.302
weapon: Wall clock (used to strike the victim on the head)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (victim's granddaughter PW-2 and her father PW-1); medical (PW-10, PW-11); recovery of stolen ornaments (PW-13); hostile neighbour witnesses PW-3 and PW-5 placing accused near the house
aggravating_circumstances: Elderly and frail victim dragged from her cot and struck on the head; child threatened and robbed; victim died
mitigating_circumstances: Accused went to the house intending robbery, not to kill; this was why the s.449 conviction was not sustained
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.449 (10 years and fine), s.397 (7 years and fine) and s.302 (life imprisonment); sentences concurrent
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed (Crl. A. No. 835 of 2004, judgment 30.10.2007); conviction and sentence upheld
offence_finally_established: IPC s.397 (robbery with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt); IPC s.302 (murder)
neutral_facts: On a day in October 1997, the accused and a companion went to a family's residence intending to commit robbery. While the companion stood guard outside, the accused entered and found the eleven-year-old daughter of the household. He caught hold of her neck, threatened to kill her, and robbed her of a gold chain and two gold ear studs. He then entered a bedroom where the victim, an elderly woman aged about 90, lay on a cot and tried to take her ornaments. When the victim raised an alarm, the accused pulled her down from the cot and struck her on the head with a wall clock. He broke a gold chain from her neck and took two imitation bangles from a bag in an almirah, then left. The girl told her father, and they returned with friends. The victim was taken to a government hospital and then a medical college hospital, where she died nine days after the incident. The treating civil surgeon recorded a forehead injury with suspicion of fracture and eyelid swelling, consistent with a wall clock blow. A forensic doctor attributed death to the head injuries. The girl gave consistent eyewitness testimony corroborating her father. Two neighbours, both declared hostile, admitted seeing the accused near the house that day. The investigating officer recovered the stolen gold ornaments at the accused's instance. No test identification parade was held. The girl identified the accused in court.
physical_harm: Head injuries to the 90-year-old victim (forehead injury with suspected fracture, eyelid oedema, lacerated forehead); victim died on 29 October 1997 from head injuries
number_of_offences: 3 charged; 2 finally upheld (ss.397 and 302); s.449 not upheld
financial_property_loss: Gold chain (about 5.500 grams) and two gold ear studs from PW-2; gold chain of about 5.500 grams from the victim; two imitation bangles taken from an almirah bag
premeditation_planning: No premeditated killing found; the court found the visit was made with a common intention to commit robbery, not to kill
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of PW-2 (victim's granddaughter); PW-1's consistent testimony; medical evidence of PW-10 and PW-11 on cause of death; recovery of gold ornaments at the accused's instance; hostile witnesses PW-3 and PW-5 on presence near the house
witness_credibility: PW-2 found credible as a victim witness; her evidence clear and unambiguous, nothing adverse elicited in cross-examination; six-year delay in recording evidence did not cause memory to fade; she was no longer a child witness
post_offence_conduct: Recovery of stolen gold ornaments at the accused's instance on 24 October 1997; no other post-offence conduct noted
trial_duration: offence: 20 October 1997; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 30 October 2007; Supreme Court: 21 November 2012
legal_representation: Accused: Purnima Bhar; State: Liz Mathew and Sana Hasmi
investigation_status: Investigation completed; charge sheet (challan) filed; trial completed; recovery of ornaments made
procedural_irregularity: No test identification parade held; the Supreme Court found the identification was dealt with in a cursory manner by the trial court and High Court; PW-2's evidence was recorded about six years after the incident
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss.449, 397 and 302 IPC. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence upheld. Supreme Court: partly allowed; s.449 conviction set aside, ss.397 and 302 upheld
prosecution_argument: Not separately recorded in the judgment; the court noted that the prosecution's case was that the accused went to the house to commit robbery
defence_argument: No TIP was held, so PW-2's evidence could not be relied on; a child witness's evidence should be carefully scrutinised; the accused had no intention to murder, so the s.302 conviction was improper
legal_principle_applied: Failure to hold a TIP is not fatal, but the trial judge must be circumspect when a stranger is identified in court; victim evidence is given a higher pedestal; murderous intent may be inferred from the act; s.449 requires intent to commit an offence punishable with death
precedent_relied_upon: Sk. Hasib v. State of Bihar, AIR 1972 SC 283; Vaikuntam Chandrappa v. State of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 1960 SC 1340; Rameshwar Singh v. State of J&K, (1971) 2 SCC 715; Budhsen v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (1970) 2 SCC 128; Malkhansingh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (2003) 5 SCC 746; Vijay @ Chinee v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (2010) 8 SCC 191; State of Himachal Pradesh v. Lekh Raj, (2000) 1 SCC 247
sentencing_rationale: Sentence not revisited. The s.449 conviction was set aside because the house trespass was for robbery, not for an offence punishable with death; ss.397 and 302 convictions upheld
judicial_aggravating_factors: Frail, elderly victim dragged from her cot and struck on the head; the court held the accused could not have been unaware that death would result
